summary: Discovery focused on reliability, fallback policies, multi-region routing, and SLA expectations. Action: send SLA matrix, run bench, schedule deep technical test.
transcript:
00:00 Ava: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Ava from Redwood, i'm the account exec on this one. um quick roll call?
00:06 Priya: hi priya here, cto at horizon.
00:09 Ethan: ethan, platform eng.
00:11 Marta: marta, security.
00:13 Liam: liam chen, solutions engineer with redwood.
00:15 Samir: samir, data eng. jules on product joining in a bit.
00:20 Ava: awesome, thanks. goal for today is to understand your reliability needs and incident tolerance expectations, mainly around fallback policies, multi-region routing, and what SLAs you need. we'll do quick context then dig into failure modes.
00:35 Priya: great, our primary use case is real-time enrichment for our analytics pipeline, inference for entity resolution and scoring. latency is pretty important, p95 ideally below 200-250ms for the short text path, p99 we can tolerate up to 600ms. cost matters but reliability and predictable behavior matter more for us.
00:52 Ethan: we're running on aws, EKS with k8s and use cross-region replication for some services. currently using a mix of OpenAI hosted endpoints and a small internal host for privacy-sensitive data. trying to decide whether to go hosted redwood, dedicated, or private.
01:10 Ava: thanks that's helpful. quick question on throughput: what's your steady qps and burst?
01:16 Samir: steady about 120 req/s, spikes up to 500 for reporting windows. typical prompt sizes are 60-150 tokens.
01:26 Ava: good. on security side Marta, what are must-haves?
01:30 Marta: SOC 2, SAML SSO integration, audit logs, KMS integration for keys, data residency options for eu, and ability to show retention settings. also need to know whether logs leave our vpc in private deployment.
01:43 Liam: all reasonable. Redwood Hosted supports SOC 2, SSO, and region-specific hosting. Dedicated gives you reserved pools and VPC peering, Private (on-prem or vpc) keeps control in your network and keys.
01:55 Priya: on reliability. what happens during a regional outage? how do fallbacks work? we can't have a blackout that impacts customer-facing dashboards.
02:04 Liam: good question. we have multi-tier fallbacks. first, request-level routing prefers the configured region; if capacity or health checks fail we automatically route to a secondary region with compatible model variant. fallback can be configured to prefer same model family but lower-cost quantized variant to preserve latency. there is also a model-variant fallback to a smaller model if the primary is overloaded.
02:30 Ethan: are those fallbacks instantaneous? what's the routing time and how do you avoid cold-start spikes?
02:36 Liam: routing is near-instant at the control plane level (tens to low hundreds ms). cold-starts are mitigated by warm pools and continuous batching on dedicated; hosted maintains warm instances for active customers. in heavy failover we recommend a short-lived degraded mode where responses are slightly slower but still served.
02:53 Priya: acceptable, but we need deterministic behavior. can we pin to no cross-region routing for certain endpoints?
02:59 Ava: yes, we support per-route routing policies. you can pin endpoints to region-only, allow region-first fallback, or global. we'll include an example policy in the docs we send.
03:10 Marta: SLA expectations—what uptime numbers do you commit for Hosted vs Dedicated?
03:14 Ava: Hosted has a standard uptime target (we'll attach exact SLA matrix) typically in the 99.9% range for API availability; Dedicated comes with higher committed SLOs and optional SLA add-ons, usually 99.95% and above depending on contract and reserved capacity. Private is dependent on your infra but we offer operational runbooks and can backstop with support SLAs for the control plane.
03:36 Priya: what's the definition of availability in the SLA? does it include regional failures and failover time?
03:41 Ava: SLA typically measures successful API responses within a configured timeout; we also specify maintenance windows and exclusions. failovers count, but we document RTO/RPO expectations and runbooks. we'll send the exact legal terms; for sales discovery we provide the numbers.
03:53 Samir: about data consistency: when routing to a different region, does the request payload or logs contain customer PII? are we ok with data transiting other regions?
04:02 Liam: there's a setting for data residency; you can enforce region-only processing. if you allow cross-region failover, data will route through the secondary region and may be subject to that region's residency. for Private deployment your data never leaves your VPC unless you choose otherwise.
04:18 Marta: KMS integration—if keys are customer-managed, do you decrypt in your control plane?
04:24 Liam: for Hosted we can integrate with BYOK using major cloud KMS options; keys are used at the model serving layer, and we don't persist plaintext keys. for Private you fully manage keys. we'll share an architecture diagram.
04:36 Priya: let's talk incident tolerance mechanics—if you lose an entire data center or region, how do you ensure requests still succeed? are there active-active setups?
04:44 Liam: we run active-active for critical regions for Dedicated and Private customers who configure it. for Hosted we maintain active-active for major regions but capacity is shared across tenants; for higher isolation you pick Dedicated. failover strategies include multi-region routing with health checks, cross-regional KV cache warmup for hot keys, and model warm-cache replicas to reduce cold starts.
05:08 Ethan: cross-regional KV cache sounds tricky. how do you keep the KV cache in-sync?
05:13 Liam: we don't replicate heavy KV state synchronously. instead we use prefix caching and heuristics: hot-prefixes can be proactively warmed in the secondary region, and we accept eventual consistency for KV cache so correctness for stateless inference isn't impacted. for stateful cached sessions we recommend session stickiness or configure a shared cache via your VPC peering.
05:34 Priya: reduction of correctness is acceptable as long as we document the failure modes.
05:38 Ava: absolutely. in the playbook we'll outline degraded behaviors: slightly higher latency, possibly falling back to smaller model with slightly different outputs, and recommendations for client-side retries and idempotency keys.
05:52 Marta: can we see traceability—end-to-end tracing and per-token cost? we need to audit who accessed what and when.
05:59 Liam: Redwood Console provides per-request traces, token-level cost breakdowns, and audit logs. you can export logs to your SIEM or S3. for Dedicated we enable richer retention and tracing hooks.
06:12 Samir: what about black swan events—if a broad internet outage causes us to lose connectivity to region, do you support degraded local-serving or queueing?
06:22 Liam: you can configure client-side fallback to a local small model, with server-side fallbacks to quantized variants. we also support queuing with retry/backoff on the client SDK. for mission-critical dashboards we recommend a hybrid where private lightweight model runs inside your VPC as a hard fallback.
06:40 Priya: can you give an example policy you'd recommend for our use case?
06:45 Liam: sure. region-first routing for primary endpoints, allow secondary-region fallback for non-PII endpoints, model-variant fallback to quantized family for spikes, and client-side 3-second timeout with exponential backoff. include sticky session cookie for 30s to keep routing pinned during bursts. we'll send the sample policy.
07:04 Ava: i want to call out costs: fallback to a secondary region or larger instance will increase cost; where possible we recommend burst capacity or autoscale rules on dedicated to minimize cross-region calls.
07:15 Ethan: can you guarantee performance for the 200-250ms p95?
07:18 Liam: with dedicated reserved capacity and correct batching configuration we commonly hit sub-200ms p95 for short prompts. for hosted customers with varying load, we aim for similar but it's less guaranteed unless you add reserved capacity. we'll include benchmark data.
07:34 Priya: testing—what's the path for us to validate?
07:37 Liam: we suggest a pilot: 2-week bench on your traffic patterns, run failover tests (bring down region or simulate capacity loss), measure p95/p99, and gather output quality checks. Redwood SE will help run the tests.
07:50 Ava: okay next steps recap: we'll send SLA matrix, routing examples, benchmark playbook, and schedule the 60-min SE deep-dive.
07:58 Marta: please also send the security questionnaire answers and any SOC2 reports you can share.
08:04 Priya: timeline wise, decision in next 6-8 weeks, pilot asap after NDA and legal review.
08:09 Ava: understood. any other questions?
08:12 Samir: curious—do you support canary rollbacks for model updates?
08:15 Liam: yes, rollout and canary policies are built-in. you can do A/B with automatic rollback on perf or quality regressions.
08:23 Jules: joining now, quick Q: what's the developer experience for switching from OpenAI endpoints?
08:27 Ava: we have SDK adapters and mapping guides; usually it's a few days to swap some calls and test. we'll share migration notes.
08:36 Priya: thanks, that's it from us. appreciate the detail.
08:39 Ava: thanks everyone we'll follow up with the docs and next-step invites. bye.
08:44 (call ends)
